replying_to: Replying to SAU: Smooth activation function using convolution with approximate identities
display_title: Official Review of Paper3309 by Reviewer VAt9

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors introduce an activation function (SAU) based on smoothing of the leaky relu. More precisely, the authors use convolutions and approximate identities to achieve that goal. 
Furthermore, they present the smooth version as a learnable activation function, whose parameters can be optimized via back-propagation and hyper-parameter searches. 
The authors present the smoothing from the ground up and conclude their theoretical development with the gradients needed for back-propagation as well as a proof that guarantees the activation function allows the network to be an universal approximator.
The empirical section describes the behavior of SAU on different datasets and architectures.
content.main_review:
The paper is technically sound and in general well written. I very much like the clever approach to smoothing and the empirical results seem very beneficial. There are however some concerns regarding the contribution and its development.

The paper presents a smoothing of the leaky relu based on convolutions and approximate identities. However, there are other smooth approximations to the leaky relu [1], consider for instance:

$SLR(\alpha, x) =  \alpha x + (1-\alpha)\log(1+e^x)$

given this pre-existing smoothing, what is this paper providing as contribution?
Is it that SAU is closer to the original leaky relu than SLR is? This could be shown by computing the integral of the squared difference between SAU and leaky relu, and then comparing to the difference between SLR and leaky relu. 
I computed that for SLR and leaky relu with an alpha=0.25 and the integral of that difference from -1000 to 1000 is 0.33, which is pretty tight. Could you show the same for SAU? is it maybe tighter? 

Is it that SAU is learnable? so is the parametric leaky relu and other learnable activation functions that can approximate the leaky relu. But is SAU special in its parametric form somehow?
We can see empirically that SAU has benefits, but are those benefits coming from the smoothing or from being learnable? an ablation experiment could help with that. You should also do a comparison to other learnable activation functions, to see how SAU stacks against modern activations.
Any ideas of what causes the improvements? could it be that the gradients provided by SAU are higher/better than the gradients of leaky relu?

All those questions point to the same concern. I believe the idea is good, but the paper needs a bit more development and it is not ready for publication as it is.

There are other minor suggestions:
In Fig. 1, you are wasting lots of useful space. I suggest you have two plots instead, one on the left with a range of -25 to 25 or larger, and another on the right zooming in around 0, to properly show the difference between the kink and the smoothing. This way you show that SAU behaves like leaky relu on the large range and show also your contribution on the smoothing.

In the introduction you have the sentence “Activation functions are usually hand-crafted”, but you also mention that earlier. Maybe you want to mention that only once?

there is a typo on the experiments section “nest sections” -> next

[1] https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/329776/approximating-leaky-relu-with-a-differentiable-function
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe the paper has a lot of potential, but there are some concerns about the characterization and benefits of SAU especially given the existing smoothing versions of the leaky relu.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3309 by Reviewer VAt9

content.title: Respond to Reviewer
content.comment:
We thank you for the time, valuable comments, and feedback.

Yes, SAU gives a tighter approximation to Leaky ReLU than the SLR approximation. We computed the integral of the squared difference (ISD) from -1000 to 1000 between Leaky ReLU and SAU, and it is 0.14 while the ISD between Leaky ReLU and SLR is 0.33. We also compute the integral of the mod difference (IMD) from -1000 to 1000 between Leaky ReLU and SAU, and it is 0.625 while the IMD between Leaky ReLU and SLR is 1.23. Also, the fact is clear if we plot curves of SLR, SAU, and Leaky ReLU for the same alpha. The SAU curve lies in between the curves of SLR and Leaky ReLU. Also, we run experiments with SLR as an activation function in different datasets, and its performance is worse than SAU.


SAU can be used as a learnable or hyperparametric activation function depending on how the user chooses alpha and n. We have chosen alpha trainable and n as a constant hyperparameter. SAU can be seen as a special parametric function as the parameter alpha controls the slope in the negative axis, which can interpolate between ReLU and Leaky ReLU. By increasing the value of n, we can make SAU closer to Leaky ReLU or ReLU (depending on alpha). We have run experiments with SAU without trainable parameters, and it boosts the performance of Leaky ReLU. SAU with trainable parameters, network performance, gets better than SAU compared to constant hyperparameters. So from empirical evaluation, it is pretty clear that there is an advantage of using differentiable approximation with trainable parameters. We have considered three trainable activations to compare our performance, Swish, Parametric ReLU (PReLU), and PAU [1]. We have initialised parameters for Swish and PReLU at 1.0 and 0.25, respectively, while the parameters of PAU are initialized as suggested in [1]. Differentiable approximation could be a possible reason for boosting the network performance (Swish, GELU, and PAU activations support this fact), and we are also interested in finding the theoretical reason behind it.

Thank you for pointing out the typo; we have updated it and updated figure 1 according to your suggestions.

[1] Padé Activation Units: End-to-end Learning of Flexible Activation Functions in Deep Networks, ICLR 2020.

content.title: Good feedback
content.comment:
I’m happy to read the comment by the authors. This makes me believe the activation function is interesting and also gives further support to the idea that the form of the gradient might indeed be helpful for learning of DNNs.
As new activation functions show up we hit a barrier of diminishing returns, but this paper provides an interesting approach that I believe is worth seeing by the rest of the community. 

I would strongly suggest that you incorporate the feedback of the review and your responses in the paper, even if just in the supplemental.
As you have addressed my concerns in a way that shows the benefits of the paper, I will raise my score. However, I still think that finding a mathematical proof or at least a strong indication that explains why the activation is better would make the paper significantly stronger.

replying_to: Replying to SAU: Smooth activation function using convolution with approximate identities
display_title: Official Review of Paper3309 by Reviewer gQcZ

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new activation function for deep neural networks. Through the lens of *approximate identities*, the authors come up with the new activation function which is a ``smoothed'' version of ReLU/Leaky ReLU, i.e., the Smooth Activation Unit (SAU). The authors conduct experiments on both vision (including classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation) and natural language processing tasks (machine translation) and compare the performance of the proposed SAU with previous widely used activation functions.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

1. The 'convolution with approximate identities' method is simple and intuitive, which could serve as a good smooth approximation for ReLU/Leaky ReLU activation functions.

Weaknesses:

1. My main concern is the empirical performance of the new activation function proposed in this paper. Specifically, the SAU is marginally better (<1.0%) than other activation functions on most of the tasks considered in this paper. Meanwhile, Table 2 and Table 3 only consider ReLU as the baseline and ignore other widely used activation functions. Outperforming ReLU on CIFAR datasets is not very convincing, since the datasets are not very challenging and SAU also has more parameters (could be further optimized) than ReLU. On the other hand, there are several widely used activation functions are smooth, for example GELU, and the SAU performs similar as GELU.

Suggestions and questions:

1. The optimizers used on CIFAR and TinyImageNet are different. It would be better to apply the same optimizer for the same task. 

2. The hyperparameters are not well tuned, for example, the initial learning rate=0.1 is widely used for vision classification tasks. It would be more convincing to consider more learning rates than just one learning rate.

3. I would like to suggest the authors explore other metrics (beyond in-distribution accuracy/mAP/mIOU/BLUE). For example, does SAU perform better in terms of model robustness? Since the smoothness may have some advantages on model robustness. 

4. What is the Lipschitz smoothness for SAU (with different $\alpha$-parameter)? This might be useful for analyzing some properties of the DNNs.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed new activation function is simple and intuitive, but the empirical performance is not very convincing.

content.title: Respond to Reviewer
content.comment:
We thank you for the time, valuable comments, and feedback.

We have a different perspective to propose SAU. We know that GELU and Swish are smooth approximations of ReLU. Swish [1] was found by a neural architecture search, and search space may be huge (depending on the core unit), which may create a computationally infeasible search space. Instead, we want to explore how the smooth approximation of Leaky ReLU/Parametric ReLU changes the dynamics and performance of a network. SAU contains two parameters, alpha and n, which can be used as hyperparameters or trainable parameters where alpha controls the slope in the negative axes. The baseline table shows that SAU beats the other baseline activations in most of the deep learning tasks. Also, we got almost 3% improvement compared to all baseline activations on the CIFAR100 dataset in the ShuffleNet V2 model, a state of the art network in ECCV2018.

We have updated the results with the SGD optimizer for the Tiny ImageNet dataset.
We tried all possible initial learning rates from the set {0.1, 0.01, 0.001} with different weight decay rates, and we noticed that on MNIST, FMNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR datasets with initial learning rate 0.01 comes out to be the best choice with 5e^-4 weight decay.

We did not ignore the other baseline activations for comparison on CIFAR datasets (in Table2 and Table3). SAU is compared with the other baseline activation functions as well. Due to page restrictions, all the results were reported in the appendix section (please see subsection A.3, Table 12-Table15). 

These are indeed a very intriguing direction that we didn't initially explore in our paper, and we will take it up in our future work.


[1] Searching for activation Functions.

content.title: Thanks for the response

I still think this paper needs to conduct extensive/large-scale experiments to demonstrate the benefits of the proposed activation. I keep my previous recommendation score. I would suggest the authors explore the advantages of the proposed activation on more challenging tasks in the future.

replying_to: Replying to SAU: Smooth activation function using convolution with approximate identities
display_title: Official Review of Paper3309 by Reviewer UwNK

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new activation function, named SAU, which is a smoothed approximation to Leaky/PReLU. The activation is derived by convolving a given activation function with a smooth approximation to the delta function. The paper only investigates using LeakyReLU as the target activation and the standard concentrated Gaussian approximation to the delta function. The degree of approximation is controlled via a hyperparameter denoted by $n$, controlling the variance of the Gaussian. The new activation is tested in various settings and with various architectures and is shown to outperform other alternatives to the common ReLU activation function.
content.main_review:
Main strengths:
* The new activation function is extensively tested under various settings and using several architectures, suggesting the new activation to be a "plug-and-play" replacement.
* SAU is shown to outperform other activation functions in almost all cases, and some by a significant margin.
* The approach for deriving a smooth approximation to LeakyReLU, while not novel, is somewhat interesting as it connects GELU and LeakyReLU together. However, this is not explored in the paper.

Main weaknesses:
* No source code is supplied for reproducing results. This is a crucial ommison in an emperical paper such as this one, making it harder to assess the validity of the reported results.
* Experiments suggest the new activation function to be less expressive than other methods. This is apparent from the loss curves that show SAU to have a higher train loss throughout training. This is in contrast to what is written in the article, where it is said SAU converge faster but the curve clearly show a slower convergence. This could also be the reason why it outperforms the other activation functions, as it might be a simple case of overfitting -- but further investigation is required.
* Despite the fact the reported experiments report SAU outperforms other activation functions, it is very difficult to say if SAU is the reason why the results are slightly better.
* Using n = 20000, as used in the reported experiments, would seem to suggest that the activation function will act exactly like LeakyReLU (PReLU), and yet it seems to still have an effect in experiments. In fact, substituting this value in the formulas in the paper would result in almost no contribution from the additional terms. If indeed this value was used and any difference in results was observed, I would highly suspect some mistake in the implementation. Access to the source code would be beneficial in this respect.
* The paper offers no argument, other than empirical results, to why this specific activation function should be preferred to other similar choices. If there's no theoretical argument, then some empirical investigation should be done to try and differentiate between this activation function and others.


Not strictly a disadvantage, but I think it's important to note that when n is small, the proposed activation is very close to GELU. In fact, one could say that this activation is an interpolation between GELU and LeakyReLU, where n controls which activation it is more similar to. The paper makes not mention of this fact, and this might be the most interesting part of this derivation and a missed opportunity. Moreover, the formula for GELU in the appendix is incorrect. The formula as written is for the approximation of computing GELU, not GELU itself. GELU is equal to $\frac{x}{2}\left(1 + \mathrm{erf}(x/\sqrt{2})\right)$, where is SAU is equal (when n=1) to GELU(x) + N(x), where N(x) is the standard normal distribution.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Despite the large empirical evaluation of the proposed activation function, the overall empirical significance of the results is only marginal, and it is hard to say if the better performance should be attributed to the activation function rather than the specific choice of hyperparameters. Specifically, I'm suspecting the benefits are due to the lower expressiveness of the proposed method leading to better generalization, which would suggest smaller models should have been used for the other activation functions. Moreover, the reported value of n is suspicious and could suggest an issue with the implementation. Finally, for such an empirical paper having access to the source code is critical for proper evaluation, and it would also be helpful for looking into the previously raised issue.

Overall, I think the paper is not yet ready for publication in its current state. Nevertheless, the derivation does have an interesting property of connecting GELU and LeakyReLU, and perhaps that should be further explored in the next revision of the paper.

content.title: Respond to Reviewer
content.comment:
We thank you for the time, valuable comments, and feedback.

We notice that there is no problem with step decay or cyclic learning rate (lr) scheduler, but with cosine annealing [5] learning rate scheduler, the convergence speed of SAU is a little slow. We reported results with cosine annealing lr as it provides better results on the MNIST, FMNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR datasets with any baseline activations than other lr scheduling methods.


It is known that Swish [1] and GELU [2] are smooth approximations [3] of ReLU, while PAU [4] is a smooth approximation of Leaky ReLU and experimental evaluations for these works shows that all of them boost the network performance of ReLU or Leaky ReLU.  

We have run experiments with SAU without trainable parameters, and it boosts the performance of Leaky ReLU. SAU with trainable parameters, network performance gets better than SAU with constant hyperparameters. So from empirical evaluation, it is pretty clear that there is an advantage of using differentiable approximation with trainable parameters. We agree that we are not able to provide a direct mathematical proof of why the smooth approximation boosts network performance, and we are also equally interested in this problem. 



Approximate identity gives a smooth version of a non-smooth function. Irrespective of the value of n, the approximate function will still be smooth in the neighbourhood of the non-differentiable point.

We note that in the last statement, the reviewer commented that SAU is GELU+N(x) when n=1, where N(x) is the standard normal distribution; however, to arrive at this conclusion, we need to assume alpha = 0 along with n=1 additionally. If alpha = 0, it means we are switching off the negative component of Leaky ReLU, reducing it to ReLU, and it is a well-known fact that GELU can be seen as a smooth approximation of ReLU. GELU is a fixed activation function, while our proposal can smoothly interpolate between ReLU or Leaky ReLU (depending on the value of alpha), and SAU can be used as a fixed or trainable activation function depending on alpha and n.

We have updated the formula of GELU in the appendix. Thank you for pointing it out.

[1] Searching for activation functions.
[2] Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs).
[3] Activate or not: Learning customized activations, CVPR 2021.
[4] Padé Activation Units: End-to-end Learning of Flexible Activation Functions in Deep Networks, ICLR 2020.
[5] SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts, ICLR 2017.

content.title: Respond to Reviewer
content.comment:
We thank you for the time, valuable comments, and feedback.

ReLU, Leaky ReLU or its variants are non-differentiable at 0. We want to explore how the smooth approximation of these well-known activation functions changes the training dynamics and network performance. From the detailed experimental evaluation, it is pretty clear that there is an advantage of using the differentiable approximation. The idea of using differentiable approximation was used earlier in Softplus and Pade activation units (PAU) [1] papers. Softplus does not perform quite well in most cases (see [2]), while PAU usually performs better than ReLU or its variants and other well-established activations in image classification problems. PAU activation contains a large number of trainable parameters, which increases the complexity of a network, while with a smaller number of trainable parameters, SAU performs quite well compared to all baseline activations and PAU on a wide range of deep learning problems. We have included all the results for PAU in the current version of the paper.
In CIFAR results, SAU is compared with the other baseline functions as well. Due to page restrictions, all the results were reported in the appendix section (please see subsection A.3, Table 12-Table15). 

[1] Padé Activation Units: End-to-end Learning of Flexible Activation Functions in Deep Networks, ICLR 2020.
[2] Deep Sparse Rectifier Neural Networks.
